title: Toughness admired
core: All five approve of holding up under force — and the exam counts on you accepting "tough = tough" and stopping there. They differ on three axes: whether the blow actually lands, whether the strength is structural or moral, and whether it's a property of a thing or a record earned by a person over time. One repels the force, one bends and returns, one absorbs it silently for years. Get the axis right and the answer choices separate cleanly.

words.nuance: The only verb here, and the only one that takes the attacking force as its direct object — a siege, 200 mph winds, scrutiny, temptation. It reports on the *force*: it pushed, and it failed. Says nothing about what the holding cost you.

A property of a built thing — a system, an economy, an argument, a body — meaning it keeps *functioning* under stress, not merely surviving it. Note the technical-prose habitat (robust growth, robust findings) and the flavour sense (robust coffee) that the other four have no version of.

The only one that concedes the damage. The blow lands, the shape deforms — and then it springs back. Calling a person or an economy resilient quietly admits they've already been through something; the others imply nothing was ever broken.

A noun, and the only purely *moral* one: strength of mind, not structure. Reserved for pain borne over duration with quiet dignity — the long illness, the grinding trial — never the ten-second act of nerve. Formal and warm, the register of eulogies.

The only one about *loyalty* and time served, and the only one that works as a noun for a person: a stalwart of the party. It praises immovability where *stubborn* condemns it, and it requires a track record — a brilliant newcomer can be robust or resilient but never stalwart.

exam_note: Sentence-equivalence traps pair **resilient** with **robust** as if interchangeable: check whether the passage says the damage already landed (resilient) or that the thing held without breaking (robust) — and if the blank is a person praised for years of loyal service, only **stalwart** fits.
